newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK CBANK SAYS PRIVATE SECTOR DEBT RISES - PAPER.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK CBANK SAYS PRIVATE SECTOR DEBT RISES - PAPER.

text.p: Slovakia's foreign debt, according to preliminary figures, increased by some $1.2 billion in 1996, a senior central bank official said on Monday.
"It is not related to the public sphere, the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) and the government, but to the private sector," NBS vice-governor Marian Jusko told the daily Pravda in an interview.
Jusko said the central bank has been noticing some negative trends which were leading to a decrease in export abilities and to a rise of the import demands of the Slovak economy.
"We need to change it," he said. "The central bank can, for example, assist (in reversing infavourable development) by influencing the activities of the commercial banks."

According to preliminary figures, the amount of domestic loans increased by more than 60 billion crowns the last year, including a 50 billion increase in the loans provided to enterprises and individuals, Jusko said.
"The increase in purchasing power, imposed by the newly-provided loans, contributed to impressive GDP growth," he said.
"But on the other hand, it helped bring a considerable deficit in the trade balance...These (contrasting) effects, considering the results of the current account, are urging us to caution," he added.
Jusko said the NBS had "basicaly" expected the recent jump in interbank money market rates to above 20 percent as one of the painful effects of the NBS's 1997 monetary programme.

"(But) we had assumed the commercial banks would accomodate the monetary program of NBS immediately after it was announced in December, and not a month later," he said, adding this was the reason why rate volatility occurred so quickly.
Jusko said he considered it possible for considerable GDP growth along with an improvement in trade to co-exist.

"But it would not be possible without... a cautious monetary policy," he said. "The matter is to adopt the corrections, which would cut the risks and bring the economy back to a well-balanced status...not over-heated but also not under-cooled," Jusko said.
